findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns
findings.body: The goroutine derives its context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. Create returns immediately after the storage write, and net/http cancels the request context when ServeHTTP returns. The legacy Create therefore usually runs with an already-cancelled context, and SQL-backed legacy stores abort the write. The resulting error is only recorded in a metric, so the legacy copy silently diverges. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The fix is to detach the context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before adding the 10s timeout.

findings.title: Legacy Update recomputes the update from the same objInfo, so legacy can persist a different object than unified
findings.body: The previous implementation computed the updated object once and handed the same result to both stores. This version passes the raw objInfo to d.Storage.Update and then, in a goroutine, to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy call invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject a second time, against the legacy store's current object, and after the handler may have returned. A patch-style or stateful UpdatedObjectInfo can then yield a different result than the one written to unified storage, so the two stores diverge with no error surfaced.

findings.title: Errors from async legacy writes are discarded without logging
findings.body: In the Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection goroutines the legacy error is only passed to a duration metric as a boolean (e.g. line 56 errObjectSt != nil). The error value and the object identity are never logged. The previous synchronous code logged these failures. Operators have no way to find which objects failed to reach legacy storage, which matters because this is the only signal that the 'safe measure' copy is missing data.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order relative to later writes
findings.body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object ordering. A Create followed quickly by a Delete of the same name can run the legacy Delete before the legacy Create. The Delete then hits NotFound (ignored), and the Create lands, leaving a legacy copy of an object that unified storage has already deleted. Update/Delete races can similarly leave resurrected or stale legacy objects. Nothing reconciles these because the error is not surfaced.

findings.title: Untracked goroutines have no panic recovery and Destroy does not wait for them
findings.body: The legacy goroutines have no recover(). A panic in a legacy implementation inside a goroutine terminates the whole process, whereas the previous synchronous calls ran in the request handler where net/http recovers the panic. Destroy() (lines 172-175) also tears down d.Legacy while these goroutines may still be using it, and there is no WaitGroup or other tracking to drain in-flight writes at shutdown.

findings.title: Delete passes the object name where the kind label is expected in the storage duration metric
findings.body: The call is d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The third argument is the kind/resource label used by the other calls (options.Kind). Passing the object name produces wrong metric labels and creates one time series per deleted object, which is an unbounded cardinality explosion in Prometheus.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy failures (Create and Update)
findings.body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) the error branch for the storage write calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). Failures of the unified storage write are therefore counted against legacy, which misattributes errors and sends operators to the wrong backend. These should be recordStorageDuration calls.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy duration as a storage duration
findings.body: The goroutine at line 166 calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). The legacy latency and error are attributed to the storage metric, which corrupts the storage/legacy comparison this dual-writer is meant to produce. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

findings.title: Unified NotFound now skips the legacy delete, which the previous code deliberately did not do
findings.body: The removed code tolerated IsNotFound from the storage Delete and still deleted from legacy. This version returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so a NotFound from unified never reaches legacy. An object that exists only in legacy stays there forever. A later Create succeeds in unified, and its async legacy Create fails with AlreadyExists, silently. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR and needs an explicit decision and a test.

findings.title: Delete attaches the bare logger to the context, dropping name/kind/method fields
findings.body: Line 96 builds a 'log' with name, kind and method values, but line 97 stores d.Log in the context instead. Storage implementations that log via klog.FromContext therefore lose the per-request fields that the other methods (Create, Get, Update) propagate.

findings.title: Method comments describe synchronous dual writes that are no longer synchronous
findings.body: The comment on Create says it writes to LegacyStorage and Storage, and the DeleteCollection comment says it deletes from both. The legacy write is now asynchronous and its failures are not reported to the caller. The comments should say so, otherwise readers will assume legacy consistency guarantees that do not exist.

findings.title: Each write spawns an unbounded goroutine with a 10s timeout and no backpressure
findings.body: Every successful write starts a goroutine that holds the object and context for up to 10 seconds. If the legacy store is slow, goroutines and held objects accumulate proportionally to write rate with no concurrency cap or queue. This can increase memory usage and goroutine count under write load.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests share one mock between storage and legacy, so they cannot verify which backend was called
findings.body: The tests use one mock.Mock for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, so an expectation set for one backend also matches calls to the other. The Create error case sets up no storage expectation, yet passes because the legacy expectation for failingObj matches the storage call. Async legacy calls are never awaited or asserted, and there is no AssertExpectations or AssertNotCalled check. The tests therefore do not verify the core Mode 3 contract: reads hit only storage, and writes go to storage first and then to legacy.

findings.title: Test name says 'not implemented' but the case tests a storage error
findings.body: The case named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented' now exercises a normal List path where the storage mock returns an error. The name is a leftover from the old stub and misdescribes the behavior under test.

findings.title: New mode 3 integration subtests assert legacy state immediately after writes that go to legacy asynchronously
findings.body: The new 'file, mode 3' and 'unified storage, mode 3' subtests run doPlaylistTests. That helper checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoint right after k8s creates and checks legacy GETs right after k8s PUT/PATCH (for example the list at line 523 and getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a goroutine after the response, so these assertions race with it and the subtests will be flaky. The helper needs to poll or wait for legacy convergence in mode 3.

findings.title: Unrelated go.work.sum churn, including a duplicated checksum line
findings.body: The go.work.sum changes add checksum entries for grafana-azure-sdk-go, grafana-plugin-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters/sdk and others that have nothing to do with the dual-writer feature. The grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery go.mod line at 408 duplicates the unchanged line just above it. These changes look like a stale workspace file and should be dropped from this PR.
